blog_summary: The blog post highlights a severe and systemic issue in the JavaScript ecosystem: outdated and vulnerable libraries are rampant across the web. The authors (Lauinger et al.) conducted a comprehensive study of over 133K websites, revealing that 37% include at least one vulnerable JavaScript library, with delays in updates measured in years. The paper underscores the ad-hoc nature of the JavaScript library ecosystem, noting the lack of reliable vulnerability databases, security mailing lists, or clear documentation of security issues in release notes. The study also explores the complexity of library inclusion, with many sites loading multiple versions of the same library or relying on transitive dependencies (e.g., via ads or trackers) that are often more vulnerable. The median website uses a library version released 1,177 days before the latest release, illustrating a chronic lack of updates. The authors emphasize that the root causes are systemic, making quick fixes unlikely without broader changes in how libraries are managed and secured.
paper_title: Thou shalt not depend on me: analysing the use of outdated JavaScript libraries on the web
paper_abstract: —Web developers routinely rely on third-party JavaScript libraries such as jQuery to enhance the functionality of their sites. However, if not properly maintained, such dependencies can create attack vectors allowing a site to be compromised. scripts or HTML into vulnerable websites via a crafted tag. As a result, it is of the utmost importance for websites to manage library dependencies and, in particular, to update vulnerable libraries in a timely fashion. In this paper, we conduct the first comprehensive study of client-side JavaScript library usage and the resulting security implications across the Web. Using data from over 133 k websites, we show that 37 % of them include at least one library with a known vulnerability; the time lag behind the newest release of a library is measured in the order of years. In order to better understand why websites use so many vulnerable or outdated libraries, we track causal inclusion relationships and quantify different scenarios. We observe sites including libraries in ad hoc and often transitive ways, which can lead to different versions of the same library being loaded into the same document at the same time. Furthermore, we find that libraries included transitively, or via ad and tracking code, are more likely to be vulnerable. This demonstrates that not only website administrators, but also the dynamic architecture and developers of third-party services are to blame for the Web’s poor state of library management. To date, security research has addressed a wide range of client-side security issues in websites, including validation [30] and XSS ([17], [36]), cross-site request forgery [4], and session fixation [34]. However, the use of vulnerable JavaScript libraries by websites has not received nearly as much attention. In 2014, a series of blog posts presented cursory measurements highlighting that major websites included known vulnerable libraries ([25], [26], [24]).
